Problem 2

loading libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

creating data frame

study_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(path, read_csv)
  ) |> unnest(data) |> 
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    arm = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    subject_id = str_sub(files, 5, 6),
    arm = recode_values(arm, "con" ~ "control", "exp" ~ "experimental")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(arm, subject_id, week, observation)

spaghetti plot

study_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations Over Time By Participant",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )

From the spaghetti plot, it appears that subjects in the control group have have relatively stable observation values over time, while the observed outcome measure in the experimental group increases approximately linearly over time from week 1 to week 8.

Problem 3

simulated data sets

# simulation

sim_t_test = function(n = 30, mu, sigma = 5) {
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  
  sim_data |> 
    pull(x) |> 
    t.test(mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |> 
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

# loop for mu = 1,2,3,4,5,6

set.seed(1)

mu_values = 0:6
output = vector("list", 7)

for (i in 1:7) {
  
  sims = vector("list", 5000)
  
  for (j in 1:5000) {
    
    sims[[j]] = sim_t_test(mu = mu_values[i])
    
  }
  
  output[[i]] = bind_rows(sims) |> 
  mutate(mu = mu_values[i])
  
}

sim_results = bind_rows(output)

plots

sim_results |>
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(p.value < 0.05)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()+
  labs(
    title = "Power of a one-sample t-test by true mu",
    x = "True mu",
    y = "Power"
  )

As the true mean gets further away from the null of 0, power increases, as a larger effect size is easier to detect. As power approaches 1, around mu = 4, it plateaus.

full_plot = sim_results |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "All samples",
    x = "True value of mu",
    y = "Average estimate of mu"
  )

rejected_plot = sim_results |> 
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(mean_estimate = mean(estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Samples where null was rejected",
    x = "True value of mu",
    y = "Average estimate of mu"
  )

full_plot + rejected_plot

For smaller effect sizes (mu = 1-3) the average estimate among rejected tests overestimates the true mu because only samples with unusually large estimates will be reach significance. As mu increases, power approaches 1, and the
estimates are nearly all rejected so the average converges to the true value of mu.
